payload.name: Preserve Explicit Search and Attempt Details
payload.description: Use when a message describes searching for, losing, or failing to find an object or attempting something without success; preserve the specific object, duration, and unsuccessful outcome in the memory.
content: During extraction, when a speaker describes searching for or losing something (e.g., 'searching for my keys for the last half hour with no luck'), create an event/state memory that includes the exact object, the stated duration or timeframe, and the unsuccessful outcome (e.g., 'could not find').

Also include any explicitly stated recurrence (e.g., 'losing it every week') as a separate facet, but do not replace the concrete search details with only the emotional reaction or a summary like 'lost his keys.'
Stop after preserving the explicitly stated search facts; do not infer reasons, locations, or outcomes beyond what was said.

candidates.solves: During memory extraction, the agent often summarizes an explicit problem or struggle (e.g., losing an item, searching without success) into a generic emotional or event statement, dropping concrete details such as the object involved, the duration, and the unsuccessful outcome. Future questions ask about those dropped details. This skill addresses preserving explicit facts about searches and failed attempts in extraction.

payload.name: Preserve Explicitly Stated Problems and Difficulties
payload.description: When a user explicitly describes a task, search, or situation as tough, difficult, annoying, or a problem, during extraction.
content: During extraction, when the speaker explicitly labels an ongoing goal, search, or task as difficult, tough, annoying, or a problem, preserve that evaluation in the memory content instead of summarizing only the goal or preference.
Record the subject, the challenged goal, and the stated difficulty (e.g., 'finding a pet-friendly place has been tough' becomes a memory that the person had difficulty finding pet-friendly housing).
Keep the difficulty in the same candidate as the related goal or activity; do not create an extra memory solely for the emotion.
Stop after the difficulty and its object are captured; do not infer or add other unstated problems.

candidates.solves: Extraction often records a user's stated goal, preference, or ongoing activity but drops explicit evaluations that the goal is hard, tough, annoying, or a problem. Future questions asking what problems the user faced then cannot be answered from memory. This skill preserves those explicitly stated difficulties across any domain.

payload.name: Extract Expressed Aesthetic Preferences
payload.description: When a speaker explicitly says they find a place, scene, or sensory aspect beautiful, gorgeous, or otherwise appealing, during extraction.
content: During extraction, if a speaker explicitly expresses admiration or preference for a visual or sensory aspect of a place, experience, or object (e.g., 'the colors are so beautiful', 'the view is amazing'), create a durable preference memory recording the speaker as subject and the appreciated aspect as object.

Capture the aspect in the speaker's own words and resolve relative time from the message timestamp; do not require a standalone opinion sentence - the statement may occur within a suggestion, plan, or small talk.
Stop after the stated aspect; do not infer additional likes or extend the same admiration to unmentioned features.

candidates.solves: Construction agents sometimes skip explicit statements of admiration or preference when they appear inside suggestions, plans, or small talk, leaving no memory to answer later questions about what a person likes or finds beautiful.

payload.name: Capture Specifically Missed Aspects
payload.description: When a speaker expresses missing, longing, or nostalgia for a past experience or activity, during extraction.
content: During extraction, when a speaker uses miss, misses, missing, nostalgic, or longs for about a past experience, capture the exact object of that feeling, not just the broader activity.
Preserve any explicit qualifiers or descriptive phrases attached to the missed object (e.g., 'peaceful moments out in nature') so the memory answers what specifically was missed.
If the statement names both a general activity and a specific missed aspect, record both with the specific aspect as the primary object of the miss.
Stop after capturing the stated missed object and its qualifiers; do not add inferred reasons or unrelated details.

candidates.solves: Extraction often records the general activity when someone says they miss an experience, dropping the precise aspect they miss (e.g., 'the peaceful moments'). This skill ensures future memories retain the exact object and qualifiers of missing/nostalgia statements so downstream questions can be answered.

payload.name: Extract Explicit Missing or Longing Statements
payload.description: When a speaker explicitly says they miss, long for, or feel the absence of something, during extraction.
content: During extraction, if a speaker explicitly states they miss, long for, or feel the absence of something (e.g., 'I miss...', 'really missing...', 'can't do that here...'), create a separate durable state or preference memory capturing what is missed and the reason if stated.
Do not merge the missing/longing into a positive appreciation memory; keep it as its own candidate so future questions about what the speaker lacks or misses can be answered.
Capture the speaker's own words for what is missed and any explicitly stated contrast (e.g., city vs. nature); stop after one memory per distinct missed subject.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction omits explicit statements of missing or longing for something, capturing only the positive appreciation (e.g., value, enjoyment) and losing the key absence fact, so future questions about what the speaker lacks or misses cannot be answered from memory.

payload.name: Extract Online Forum Writing Participation
payload.description: Use when a message states a user joined or participates in an online forum/community and mentions discussing favorite topics there.
content: During extraction, when a user says they joined or participate in an online forum/community and describes having a talk/discussion about a topic, record the action as writing comments/posts about that topic (e.g., 'writes comments about favorite books in a fantasy literature forum').
Do not paraphrase this into a generic 'had a discussion' memory that omits the writing/participation verb.
During CRUD, when updating or merging such a memory, preserve the explicit writing-participation wording; do not replace it with a vaguer discussion summary.

Only infer writing when the forum participation is text-based and the message describes the user contributing to the discussion; if the user only mentions reading/lurking, do not infer writing, and stop after capturing the stated activity and topic.

candidates.solves: Paraphrasing an online forum discussion as a generic 'had a discussion' drops the fact that the user writes comments/posts, leaving later questions about their writing unanswered. This skill preserves the written participation action and topic in the extracted memory.

payload.name: Preserve Explicit Value Statements with Source Attribution
payload.description: Use when a speaker explicitly states a personal value, principle, or lesson they learned from a specific person and intend to keep it in mind.
content: During extraction, when a speaker explicitly states a value, principle, or lesson they learned from a specific person and says they want to keep it in mind, create a separate durable preference candidate that records the exact value and the person it came from.
Do not let a broader summary of the conversation replace this specific attributed claim; preserve the precise wording and source so the memory can answer later questions about that exact value.
Create at most one candidate per distinct value-and-source pair, and extract only values explicitly stated; do not infer additional values or generalize beyond the message.
During CRUD, process these candidates normally; no special handling is required.

candidates.solves: When a single message contains several related themes, extraction often compresses them into one generic memory and drops an explicitly stated value or lesson attributed to a specific person (e.g., a parent stressing the value of helping others). This Skill preserves such attributed value statements so later questions about that exact value can be answered.

payload.name: Extract Course and Group Enrollments
payload.description: When a user states they have taken, are taking, signed up for, or joined a course, class, workshop, training, or group, during extraction.
content: During extraction, treat any explicit statement of taking, having taken, signing up for, or joining a course, class, workshop, training, or group as a durable event candidate, even if mentioned briefly or in small talk.
Use memory kind 'event' with subject=speaker; record the exact course/class/workshop/group name as the object and set world_start from the message timestamp or stated start.
Do not require the statement to describe a physical activity with a pet or another person; structured enrollments are memory-worthy on their own.
Stop after capturing the enrollment; do not infer completion, outcomes, or related enrollments unless explicitly stated.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction sometimes misses explicit statements where a user has taken, is taking, signed up for, or joined a course, class, workshop, training, or group, especially when the active skill focuses on recreational activities rather than structured enrollments. This Skill ensures those explicit enrollments are captured as durable event memories.

payload.name: Extract Praise of Another Person's Progress
payload.description: When a speaker explicitly praises, acknowledges, or comments on another person's progress, effort, or achievement, extract it as a memory.
content: During extraction, if a message contains an explicit positive assessment of another person's progress, effort, or achievement, create a state or event candidate recording the target person, the acknowledged progress, and the speaker.
Do not skip such commentary just because it is supportive praise directed at someone else rather than the current speaker's own goal or status.
Extract only explicit acknowledgments; do not infer praise from generic encouragement or questions.

candidates.solves: Construction sometimes skips turns where a speaker comments on another person's progress, effort, or achievement, leaving no memory for later questions about what was said. This skill ensures extraction captures explicit praise or acknowledgment of another person's progress as a durable memory.

payload.name: Extract Explicit Learning Outcomes
payload.description: Use when a user mentions reading, watching, studying, or another learning activity and then explicitly states what they learned or discovered from it.
content: During extraction, if a user reports an activity such as reading books, taking a course, or watching a program, and a subsequent message states what they learned, discovered, or understood from it, create a separate memory candidate capturing the learned content with the source (e.g., 'learned X from Y').
Preserve all explicit details of the learning outcome, including specific topics and relationships; do not summarize them away or fold them only into the activity memory.
Use memory kind 'state' for durable knowledge gained; do not infer learning that was not explicitly stated.
When updating an existing activity memory that omitted the learned content, append the explicitly stated learning outcome.
Stop after capturing the stated outcome; do not expand into implications or unstated facts.

candidates.solves: When a user reports doing an activity such as reading, watching, or studying, and the conversation later states what they learned or discovered from it, extraction often records only the activity and drops the learned content, causing future recall questions to fail. This skill ensures explicit learning outcomes are captured as durable memory.

payload.name: Extract Explicit Skill-Learning Statements
payload.description: When a speaker explicitly states how they learned a skill or activity (e.g., 'I taught myself', 'I learned on my own', 'my dad taught me'), during extraction capture the learning method as a durable memory.
content: During extraction, if a speaker explicitly states how they acquired a skill or hobby (self-taught, taught by someone, learned as a child), create a candidate memory capturing that fact even when the statement answers a direct question or is embedded in a longer reply.
Record the speaker as subject and include the learning method and, if stated, the age or time period; do not require the statement to be framed as an origin story.
If self-taught, state that explicitly; if someone else taught them, name that person. Do not infer a learning method when none is stated.
Stop after capturing one memory per skill; do not combine the learning fact with unrelated activity details or add extra searches.

candidates.solves: Construction agents sometimes fail to persist explicit statements about how a person learned a skill (self-taught vs taught by others) because such statements appear as short answers to questions or are overshadowed by longer conversational topics, leaving later queries about the learning origin unanswered.

payload.name: Capture Self-Described Strategies Separately from Advice
payload.description: During extraction, when a speaker answers a request for advice by describing their own habits, practices, or strategies, create a self-referential memory for the speaker.
content: When a speaker uses first-person language ('I stay motivated by...', 'It helps me to...') in response to an advice request, create a state or event memory with subject=speaker capturing those explicit practices.
Do not fold the speaker's own practices only into an advice memory about the recipient; if the message also gives advice, capture the advice in a separate candidate.
Attribute each explicit practice to the person who performs it and stop once all explicit practices are captured.

candidates.solves: When a speaker answers a request for advice by describing their own strategies or coping mechanisms, extraction can misattribute those practices as advice given to the requester. This Skill ensures the speaker's own practices are captured as self-referential memories while separate advice is still recorded.

payload.name: Capture Stated Perspective Shifts
payload.description: Use when a user states how a book, experience, or conversation changed their perspective, thinking, or beliefs.
content: During extraction, when a user explicitly describes a change in perspective (e.g., 'made me think again', 'changed how I see', 'now I believe'), include the specific shift and any exact phrases or concepts they mention in the memory content; do not reduce it to a generic statement of motivation or inspiration.
If the user names a concept or goal central to the shift (e.g., 'personal legends'), preserve that term verbatim in the candidate content.
Capture only the stated perspective change and its immediate context; stop without inferring additional beliefs or actions.

candidates.solves: When extracting memories, summaries often reduce an explicitly stated perspective change (e.g., 'made me think again about following dreams and searching for personal legends') into a generic motivation or inspiration statement, losing the specific shift and key phrases. This skill ensures the extraction captures the exact perspective change and terminology when a user describes how a book, experience, or conversation influenced their thinking.

payload.name: Preserve Direct Quotes in Memory Candidates
payload.description: Use when a source message contains an explicit direct quote, distinctive phrase, or memorable statement from a speaker that a future question might ask about; apply during extraction to preserve the exact wording.
content: During extraction, when a speaker's message contains an explicit direct quote or distinctive memorable phrase (e.g., 'Let's live it up and make some great memories'), preserve that exact wording in the memory candidate instead of replacing it with a general summary.
When merging or updating an existing memory, keep the verbatim quote in the merged content so it remains retrievable for later questions.
Stop after preserving the quote and its speaker/context; do not duplicate the whole message or add unrelated details.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates often reduce a speaker's exact words to a paraphrase, so later questions that ask for a direct quote cannot be answered from memory. This skill keeps explicit direct quotes and memorable phrases in the stored memory content.

payload.name: Extract Stated Activity Benefits and Feelings
payload.description: When a message contains a first-person statement about what an activity, habit, or practice helps the speaker feel or why it matters to them.
content: During extraction, treat first-person statements that explain what an activity, habit, or practice helps the speaker feel or why it is important as a preference or state memory candidate.
Capture the activity and the stated benefit or feeling exactly as expressed; do not require fact-like phrasing or an explicit routine.
Create at most one candidate per activity-benefit pair, and skip if the same benefit is already captured for that activity.
Stop after capturing the stated benefit; do not infer unmentioned feelings or expand into additional memory kinds.

candidates.solves: Prevents omission of first-person statements that explain what an activity, habit, or practice helps the speaker feel or why it matters, especially when the statement is expressed as a reflective benefit rather than a plain factual assertion.

payload.name: Capture Activity Purpose and Context
payload.description: Use when a message states that someone does an activity for an explicit purpose or in a specific context, such as keeping busy, staying active, or recovering.
content: During extraction, when a speaker states they do an activity for a purpose or in a context (e.g., 'to keep me busy', 'to stay active', 'while healing'), create a memory that captures both the activity and the explicitly stated purpose/context.
Do not collapse such a statement into only a general hobby or enjoyment memory; preserve the stated reason and situation so the memory answers why the person does it.
Stop after recording the activity and its stated purpose/context; do not add inferred purposes.

candidates.solves: Extraction often stores an activity as a generic hobby or enjoyment statement, dropping the explicitly stated purpose or context (e.g., to keep busy while healing), so later memory cannot answer questions about why the person does the activity.

payload.name: Extract distinct daily-routine activities separately
payload.description: When a user describes their daily routine with time-of-day segments (morning, afternoon, evening), ensure each explicitly stated activity is captured as a separate memory candidate.
content: During extraction, when a speaker describes a daily routine using explicit time-of-day segments (e.g., in the morning, in the evenings), create one durable memory candidate per distinct stated activity or activity cluster within each segment.
Do not consolidate the whole routine into a single preference summary that could omit one segment; keep morning, afternoon/evening components as separate candidates.
Resolve relative time from the message timestamp and use memory kind 'state' for habitual routines or 'event' for one-off occurrences.
During CRUD, if a matching routine memory already exists, UPDATE or MERGE the specific segment/activity rather than replacing the whole routine summary.
Stop after capturing the explicitly stated activities; do not infer unmentioned routine components.

candidates.solves: Extraction sometimes consolidates a multi-part daily routine into one preference summary, omitting activities in other time segments (e.g., evening habits), so later questions about those activities cannot be answered. This skill solves that by requiring separate durable candidates for each explicitly stated routine activity and time segment.

payload.name: Preserve Explicit Stages and Durations in Life Narratives
payload.description: Use when a message narrates a person's history or involvement in an activity and explicitly names multiple stages (e.g., school levels, teams, jobs) or states a duration.
content: During extraction, if a narrative explicitly lists stages or levels of participation (e.g., middle school, high school, college, teams, jobs), preserve each named stage in the candidate memory instead of summarizing with a generic phrase like 'since childhood' or 'through school'.
If the narrative states a duration for a stage (e.g., 'for two years' or 'since 2015'), attach that duration to the corresponding stage in the memory.

During CRUD, when a later message adds an explicit stage or duration for an activity already in memory, UPDATE or MERGE the existing memory to include the new facts while preserving previously stored stages.
Stop after capturing every explicitly named stage and duration in the message; do not infer unstated levels, teams, or time spans.

candidates.solves: A memory extraction that paraphrases a multi-stage personal narrative into a generic summary loses explicitly named stages and durations, so later questions about which schools, teams, or jobs a person was involved with or for how long cannot be answered. This skill ensures each named milestone and time span is preserved in extracted and updated memories.

payload.name: Capture all explicit activities from multi-message events
payload.description: When creating one event memory from multiple messages about the same trip, visit, or event and later messages add explicit activities, use during extraction to preserve each distinct activity.
content: During extraction, when building a single event candidate from multiple messages about the same trip or visit, scan all source messages for explicitly named activities (e.g., excursions, classes, cafes, temples) and include each distinct one in the candidate content.
Do not drop a later explicit activity just because an earlier message already established the event; if the later message names an additional concrete activity, add it to the same memory.
Stop after all explicitly stated activities are captured; do not infer or add activities the speaker did not mention.

candidates.solves: Construction agents sometimes merge several turns about one trip or event into a single event memory and omit an explicit activity mentioned in a later turn, leaving the memory incomplete and unable to answer questions about that activity. This skill ensures every explicitly named activity in the source messages is preserved when consolidating event evidence.

payload.name: Include all explicit activities when consolidating trip memories
payload.description: When multiple messages in the same session describe the same past trip or event, use during extraction to ensure the consolidated event memory includes all explicitly mentioned activities and details from every message.
content: When extracting an event memory that consolidates multiple messages about the same trip or event, include every explicitly mentioned activity, location, or other fact from all messages; do not stop at the first message's summary.
Stop after all explicitly stated details are included; do not infer additional activities or details not mentioned in any message.

candidates.solves: When consolidating multiple messages about the same past trip or event into a single event memory, the summary can omit explicit activities or details mentioned in later messages, leading to partially covered claims.
